newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Central Europe grain surplus seen as little threat to EU.
newsitem.headline: Central Europe grain surplus seen as little threat to EU.

text.p: Fears that grain surpluses in four central European countries will cause a major problem when they join the European Union are unfounded, Hungarian grain trader Daniel Lacfi said on Thursday.
"The worries are definitely exaggerated," Lacfi told an Agra Europe grains conference.

Lacfi, president of Budapest-based Gabona Co Ltd, said that it would take up to 10 years for grain production in Hungary, Romania, Slovakia and Poland to recover to 1980 levels after disruption following the collapse of communism.
The expected export surplus of around five million tonnes, mostly wheat, in the four countries would represent only about two percent of world trade and mostly be taken by CIS states, he said.
If there is a maize surplus, it will easily be absorbed by Poland and Slovenia with some exports to Mediterranean and Black Sea ports.
The EU could consider a freight subsidy to facilitate exports from landlocked countries, such as Hungary, to cover the extra cost to the sea ports, Lacfi said.
Lacfi added that during the run-up to EU membership more emphasis should be put on restructuring agricultural production in the candidate countries to make it more complementary.
"The EU imports maize, rapeseed and sunseed which could be provided by eastern Europe," he noted.
Lacfi told Reuters that EU aid during the pre-accession period was most urgently needed to improve transport infrastructure, especially loading and unloading facilities, on the Danube.
"Waterways are the cheapest and least polluting form of transport," he said, noting their importance for shipments north to Germany and the Netherlands and south east to the Black Sea.
